evidence: Quint. 9.4.41–42: etiam monosyllaba, sī plūra sunt, male continuābuntur
terms.comment: From Greek μονοσύλλαβος, with verbum understood. Traupman’s monosyllaba, monosyllabae f. (247) takes syllaba as understood; Lewis & Short gives only the neuter.

phrases.latin: etiam monosyllaba, sī plūra sunt, male continuābuntur
phrases.english: monosyllables too, if there are several, will run badly together

sources: John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 247.
Quintilian checked against the Perseus Latin texts, and cited by its numbering.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
